United States v. Fields / Crawley; Second Circuit Nos. 96-1168 and 96-1257, 113 F.3d 313. Plenary merits decision, February 9, 1998, reviewing the Second Circuit's May 12, 1997 affirmance of both convictions. No separate Supreme Court docket or exact argument date is supplied. The question concerns observation through a five-to-six-inch gap below bedroom blinds from a shared side yard, with each defendant's personal privacy interest and the necessary entry, announcement and suppression consequences. Informant disclosure, cocaine sentencing, Fields's fine and jury selection remain outside review.

Fields repeatedly paid for access, possessed a key and could enter and bring guests; Crawley repeatedly visited with permission but had no key, payment or established overnight plan that evening. Warner respected the closed bedroom door. Officers could not see inside from the street or sidewalk. They crossed fenced rear and side areas, shared with other tenants, and saw the well-lit room without enhancement, leaning or tiptoes. After observation and without seeking a warrant, they arranged front and rear teams. A porch occupant warned of police before the planned front knock. Officers then forced the common-building rear door and entered the apartment through its open door. A later warrant and Warner's signed consent followed while the premises were secured.

Women’s Medical Professional Corp. v. Voinovich; Sixth Circuit Nos. 96-3157 and 96-3159. Plenary merits decision, April 20, 1998; October Term 1997, chunk 7. On review of the Sixth Circuit’s final judgment, 130 F.3d 187, entered November 18, 1997. No argument date or separate Supreme Court docket is supplied.

The questions are whether Casey’s abortion-review standard or Salerno’s no-valid-applications formulation governs this facial challenge; whether Ohio’s D&X prohibition fails because of its definition, clinical reach, notice or criminal and civil culpability provisions; and whether postviability law must permit necessary abortion to avert severe, lasting and potentially irreversible mental or emotional injury. The Court addresses the complete Casey standard rather than adopting an independent numerical facial threshold.

Ohio’s H.B.135 created an all-stage method prohibition, a separate postviability prohibition, viability-testing requirements and related clinical duties. The district court’s preliminary injunction became permanent on January 12, 1996 after consolidation with trial by stipulation. The Sixth Circuit sustained an injunction against the whole Act, relying on the method definition’s overlap with D&E, clinical-fault concerns, serious mental-health exclusion and inseverability. Those legal conclusions remain subject to review. The lower standing ruling and the State’s failure to contest it in the court of appeals supply no new standing holding here.

Under §2919.17(A), purposeful performance, inducement or attempted performance or inducement of an abortion on a viable fetus is prohibited unless a physician, acting in good faith and using reasonable medical judgment, determines either that abortion is necessary to prevent maternal death or a serious risk of substantial and irreversible impairment of a major bodily function, or that the fetus is not viable after the assessment required by §2919.18(A). The latter provision requires, beginning with the twenty-second week, a good-faith determination of nonviability using reasonable medical judgment, after examining the patient and performing or arranging the viability tests a reasonable physician would use. Its medical-emergency exception excuses that testing obligation. The separate twenty-four-week viability presumption is rebuttable.

Section 2919.16(F) defines the emergency through the physician’s good-faith, reasonable medical assessment of a pregnancy complication: immediate abortion must be needed to prevent the patient’s death or to avoid a serious risk, created by delay, of substantial and irreversible impairment of a major bodily function. Section 2919.16(J) separately defines that serious-risk category by a medically diagnosed condition complicating the pregnancy that directly or indirectly causes such impairment. Its nonexclusive examples are preeclampsia, inevitable abortion, prematurely ruptured membranes, diabetes and multiple sclerosis. These enacted categories remain distinct from the constitutional protection and the method-prohibition defenses addressed below.

Miller v. Albright, No. 96-1060. Plenary merits decision, April 22, 1998; October Term 1997, chunk 7. Argued November 4, 1997. On writ of certiorari to the D.C. Circuit. The question concerns unequal citizenship-transmission requirements for a child born abroad to a citizen father rather than a citizen mother.

Miller was born in the Philippines on June 20, 1970. Her November 1991 citizenship application was denied; she applied again after a July 1992 Texas decree established the biological and legal parent-child relationship with her citizen father. The State Department accepted his citizenship and sufficient physical presence to transmit citizenship. Paternity is undisputed, although no formal clear-and-convincing finding is reported. The denial expressly rested on §1409(a)(4). The father initially sued with her, was dismissed, did not appeal, and the action was transferred from Texas to the District of Columbia. The district court dismissed for lack of power to grant the requested citizenship; the court of appeals recognized standing but sustained the statutory distinction.

The amended §1409(a) separately requires clear-and-convincing proof of blood relationship; the father's United States nationality at birth; his written agreement, unless deceased, to support the person until eighteen; and, while the person is under eighteen, legitimation under residence or domicile law, his written sworn acknowledgment, or competent-court paternity adjudication. The last alternatives are disjunctive. Miller may elect the former subsection, which required legitimation before twenty-one and did not contain the later support promise. Her decree followed both age deadlines. The former route retains the separate §1401 transmission predicates; the earlier ten-year presence period, including five years after fourteen, differs from the amended five-year period, including two after fourteen. The agency accepted sufficient presence; no deficiency under either applicable version is found.

Section 1409(c) separately gives the citizen mother's nationality at birth to a person born abroad and out of wedlock after December 23, 1952 when the mother previously had continuous physical presence for one year in the United States or an outlying possession. The constitutionality of the differing presence periods and every independent support application are outside this decision. No amended support or blood-proof requirement is added to the former-law route.

Calderon v. Thompson, No. 97-215. Argued December 9, 1997; decided April 29, 1998. On review of the Ninth Circuit’s August 3, 1997 recall of its mandate in Thompson’s first federal habeas proceeding. California seeks reversal and reinstatement of the June 11 mandate denying relief.

Thompson was convicted in 1983 of murder and rape; the rape special circumstance supported death eligibility. His January 1990 federal application produced rape-related relief and vacation of the death sentence in 1995, while the murder claim was denied. A circuit panel reversed the granted relief. After January 17, 1997 notice concerning rejection of the en banc suggestion, a March 12 request for belated consideration described a law-clerk communication failure; another judge supported it, and the panel author rejected it. The mandate issued June 11.

The en banc majority later reported a separate court-initiated recall request shortly after issuance. That initiative preceded the prisoner’s July new-evidence motion but was not an entered recall or stay. The August 3 recall, after the circuit’s stated wait for state proceedings, rested on the first application’s claims and evidence and excluded the later Leitch account. It restored conditional rape-conviction and rape-special-circumstance relief and the associated death-sentence vacation, directed further murder review, and vacated the then-entered execution order.

The questions concern an ordinance permitting nonprofit organizations, but not unaffiliated individual speakers, to solicit donations and sell qualifying message-bearing merchandise on the Venice Boardwalk, and whether that distinction satisfies public-forum tailoring and alternative-channel requirements.

Ricci v. Village of Arlington Heights, No. 97-501. Argued April 21, 1998; decided May 4, 1998. On review of the Seventh Circuit’s affirmance of summary judgment, 116 F.3d 288. The question concerns the reasonableness of automatic station-house custody for operating a business without the required license, accepting probable cause and state and local arrest authority.

Officers at Ricci’s telemarketing business asked about his license, and he acknowledged having none. Under Village policy they took him to the station, locked him in an interview room for approximately an hour while preparing enforcement documents, and released him on recognizance. His wife obtained the license, and the charge was dismissed. The civil licensing ordinance carried a $5–$500 fine for each offense, with each day a separate offense; no accumulated fine is adjudicated here.

The separate premises-search claim was settled, and dismissal of the no-probable-cause claim was not appealed. A distinct warrant-clause argument first raised at appellate oral argument was held waived; Ricci conceded an arrest under a warrant would have been reasonable. The preserved question concerns the objective extent of this custody, not a revived warrant, search or probable-cause claim.

Phillips v. Washington Legal Foundation, No. 96-1578. Argued January 13, 1998; decided June 15, 1998. On writ of certiorari to the Fifth Circuit. The question is whether interest actually generated by client funds in a mandatory IOLTA account is the private property of the principal’s owner for Takings Clause purposes.

Texas requires lawyers to place client funds in IOLTA when they cannot reasonably be expected to earn interest for the client, or when expected interest would not cover the costs of establishing and maintaining the account, service charges, accounting and tax reporting. The interest goes to the Texas Equal Access to Justice Foundation to finance legal services for persons with low incomes. The District Court granted summary judgment on the ground that clients had no property interest in the proceeds. The Fifth Circuit reversed that determination and left the remaining takings questions for further proceedings.

Caron v. United States, No. 97-6270. Argued April 21, 1998; decided June 22, 1998. On writ of certiorari to the First Circuit. The question is whether §921(a)(20) preserves a conviction's federal firearms consequences when state restoration of civil rights retains a restriction on some firearm possession.

Massachusetts restored Caron's civil rights by operation of law. He held the required identification permit and could possess rifles and shotguns because the convictions were more than five years old, but could not possess handguns outside his home or business. A December 1993 search recovered six rifles and shotguns and ammunition. A jury returned four §922(g)(1) convictions. The initial enhancement counted one California and three Massachusetts convictions. After an en banc decision rejected the requirement of individualized restoration, the District Court excluded the Massachusetts convictions; the reviewed First Circuit judgment counted them because a significant firearms restriction remained.

Gebser v. Lago Vista Independent School District, No. 96-1866. Argued March 25, 1998; decided June 22, 1998. On writ of certiorari to the Fifth Circuit. The question is what showing permits private damages against a school district under Title IX for a teacher's sexual harassment of a student. Review concerns only the appealed Title IX judgment against the district.

In October 1992, parents of two other students complained to the principal about Waldrop's classroom comments. The principal met with him, received an apology and assurance against repetition, cautioned him and informed the guidance counselor, but did not transmit the complaint to the superintendent, the Title IX coordinator. Gebser did not report the relationship herself. Police discovered it in January 1993, and the district terminated Waldrop.

The evidence about grievance procedures is disputed. The superintendent's affidavit described a policy, while deposition testimony described no formal policy; she did not remember whether a handbook notifying students of procedures had been distributed. Gebser testified that she probably would have reported had she known what to do, while describing bewilderment and fear. These are evidentiary accounts, not findings of institutional fault or causation. The District Court granted summary judgment for the district, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed under an actual-supervisory-knowledge requirement.

Pennsylvania Board of Probation & Parole v. Scott, No. 97-581. Argued March 30, 1998; decided June 22, 1998. On writ of certiorari to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court. The question is whether the federal exclusionary rule applies when parole officers search their known supervisee unconstitutionally and the parole authority seeks to use the evidence in revocation.

Scott’s parole prohibited possession of weapons. Parole officers arrested him, obtained his residence keys and searched without obtaining consent; they found firearms, a bow and arrows. The Board admitted the evidence and recommitted him. The Commonwealth Court reversed, and the Pennsylvania Supreme Court affirmed that reversal on the federal exclusionary ground because the searchers knew his parole status. The Court assumes the Fourth Amendment violation for this remedial question and does not decide the validity or state-law basis of the lower court’s consent construction.

United States v. Bajakajian, No. 96-1487. Argued November 4, 1997; decided June 22, 1998. On writ of certiorari to the Ninth Circuit. The question is whether forfeiture of the entire $357,144 transported out of the country without the required report violates the Excessive Fines Clause.

Bajakajian pleaded guilty to willfully failing to report currency under 31 U.S.C. §§5316 and 5322. A separate false-statement count was dismissed by agreement, not decided by acquittal. After a forfeiture trial, the District Court found a lawful source, intended payment of a lawful debt and no connection to another crime. It refused full forfeiture under 18 U.S.C. §982(a)(1), ordered $15,000 forfeited and imposed three years’ probation and a $5,000 fine. Section 5322(a) authorized up to five years and $250,000; the applicable Guidelines maxima were six months and $5,000.

The Ninth Circuit affirmed on the ground that reporting currency was not an instrumentality and thus could not be forfeited, without reaching its proportionality prong. The Government seeks the full fund. Bajakajian did not cross-appeal the $15,000 forfeiture.

Clinton v. City of New York, No. 97-1374. Argued April 27, 1998; decided June 25, 1998. On direct appeal under 2 U.S.C. §692 from the District of Columbia's consolidated declaratory judgment, 985 F. Supp. 168. The questions concern the statutory review channel, each action's Article III standing and whether the challenged post-enactment cancellations violate Article I.

On August 11, 1997, the President canceled §4722(c) of the Balanced Budget Act and §968 of the Taxpayer Relief Act, each signed August 5. The former protected identified New York provider taxes from specified Medicaid recoupment consequences; the latter made a qualifying seller's tax deferral available for specified cooperative acquisitions. The New York plaintiffs face revived fiscal exposure. Snake River claims injury to an actual acquisition opportunity supported by identified discussions and an owner's interest in a tax-deferred sale. No completed sale or guaranteed tax benefit is found.

Swidler & Berlin v. United States, No. 97-1192. Argued June 8, 1998; decided June 25, 1998. On writ of certiorari to the District of Columbia Circuit. The question is whether the attorney-client privilege survives death and whether later criminal-investigative importance permits a case-specific override.

As investigations concerning the dismissal of White House Travel Office employees began, Vincent Foster consulted attorney Hamilton for legal representation. Hamilton made handwritten notes. Foster died nine days later. A federal grand jury, at the Independent Counsel’s request, subpoenaed the notes in an investigation concerning possible crimes during the earlier investigations. The District Court denied enforcement on privilege grounds. The court of appeals adopted a posthumous exception for communications of substantial relative importance to particular criminal litigation.

The amendment alleged a continuing official devotional practice and supported it with earlier concrete incidents; those allegations remain unproved.

Monge v. California, No. 97-6146. Argued April 28, 1998; decided June 26, 1998. October Term 1997, chunk 12. On writ of certiorari to the Supreme Court of California, reviewing 16 Cal. 4th 826, 941 P.2d 1121 (1997). The question is whether the Double Jeopardy Clause bars another attempt to establish the serious-prior-felony allegation after the first proof failed to establish its necessary personal-conduct qualification.

The jury convicted Monge of using a minor to sell marijuana, selling or transporting marijuana, and possessing marijuana for sale. The information gave notice of a serious-prior-felony allegation and a distinct prior-prison-term allegation. Monge waived a jury on those allegations. At the bifurcated bench proceeding, the State introduced a prison record establishing an assault conviction and imprisonment, but not necessarily the required personal use of a dangerous or deadly weapon or personal infliction of great bodily injury. The prosecutor's assertion about use of a stick was not evidence of that missing fact. The trial court found both allegations true and imposed eleven years: a selected five-year term doubled to ten, plus one year for the separate prison-term allegation. A three-year term on count two was stayed and a two-year term on count three ran concurrently.

The State conceded on appeal that the first record did not prove the serious-prior qualification beyond a reasonable doubt. The Court of Appeal found insufficiency and barred retrial. The California Supreme Court reversed that double-jeopardy ruling, permitting another proof proceeding. The seven-year unenhanced maximum on count one, fourteen-year qualifying-prior maximum, selected five-year term and independent one-year enhancement remain distinct.

The asserted personal responsibility of psychiatrists Hoyos and Rivera-Gonzalez and officials Diaz-Pagan, Santiago-Gonzalez and Toledo-Davila arises from their own evaluations, rearming, deployment or other alleged culpable contributions, not their titles. These are assumptions for legal review, not findings of constitutional wrongdoing.

The District Court denied the motions in a brief order before completion of the Rule 56(f) process and receipt of all oppositions. The First Circuit identified likely favorable assumptions from materials already in the trial record and excluded extra-record appellate material. Missing opposition was not a default or admission.

Brewster v. Board of Education; Ninth Circuit No. 97-55203; 149 F.3d 971. Plenary merits decision on submission, August 17, 1998; October Term 1997, chunk 12. On review under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1) of the Ninth Circuit's July 13, 1998 judgment awarding the individual officials personal damages immunity on the attendance-speech and salary-process claims. No separate Supreme Court docket or exact argument date is established.

The questions concern the particular legal speech-immunity ground, each defendant's individual position, and the independent salary-immunity grounds covering prospective reduction and reported retrospective recovery. The Court reviews those legal grounds on the proper assumptions; it does not determine disputed historical facts. The District Court's rejection of the distinct union-grievance claim, five state claims and failure-to-train claim is outside this review.

Brewster entered service as a probationary elementary teacher in September 1994. He reported attendance-accounting concerns affecting public funding, including errors to Principal Gary Furuno and a different fraud allegation to Superintendent Audrey Clarke. Furuno recommended nonrenewal on January 23, 1995. The Board met February 28, and a March notice ended service June 30. For this appeal the officials conceded attendance speech motivated Furuno and asserted no same-decision defense; those limits do not establish every fact at trial or another defendant's motive.

Assistant Superintendent Althea Jenkins initially placed Brewster at salary Step 15. Her December 2 and 7 memoranda identified deficient teaching-experience verification and a proposed Step 4 placement, invited response and preceded the December 13 Board action. Brewster and his representative met Jenkins December 15; she considered his administrative-experience argument and proposed comparator before confirming the reduction January 9, 1995. Initial entitlement and retrospective withholding are assumed. Exact withholding dates and amounts are not established.

The petitions of Metropolitan Dade County and Allied Minority Contractors Association concern the Eleventh Circuit's September 2, 1997 judgment, amended October 8, 1997, 122 F.3d 895, affirming declarations and permanent injunctions against three contracting programs. No exact Supreme Court oral-argument date is established.

The questions concern the evidence and fit required for local Black-owned (BBE), Hispanic-owned (HBE) and women-owned (WBE) construction preferences. The programs cover County-funded construction contracts over $25,000 in general building (SIC 15), heavy construction (SIC 16) and specialty trades (SIC 17), with respective 15, 19 and 11 percent goals. Eligibility requires actual local operation and covered ownership and control, normally at small-business size; a larger firm may retain certification on showing it continues to experience the addressed discrimination.

The measures include set-asides ordinarily requiring three available covered firms; with two, competitive bidding may be waived only if neither obtained a like County contract within three years and price analysis establishes a competitive price. Contract-specific subcontract goals permit waiver for unavailability at a competitive price, but not inability to obtain bonding. Project goals draw on a covered subcontractor pool. Bid preferences lower the comparison price by up to 10 percent without lowering the amount paid; selection factors may raise nonprice evaluation by up to 10 percent. Annual efficacy and five-year continuation reviews apply.

The County offered 1989–91 and 1993 contract studies, broader marketplace, subcontract, business-entry and income studies, and anecdotal accounts. Hurricane Andrew's effect led to omission of 1992. Most firm-size-adjusted award disparities disappeared; residual results differed by group, sector and year. The existing BBE program could affect observed results, but no counterfactual dataset establishes its exact effect. Anecdotal accounts were chiefly BBE, some WBE and none HBE. They are evidence offered, not findings that every incident occurred.

Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Johnson & Higgins, Inc.; No. 96-1743, petition captioned Johnson & Higgins, Inc. v. EEOC; Second Circuit No. 95-6216. Plenary merits decision on submission, September 21, 1998; October Term 1997, chunk 13. Review of the Second Circuit's August 8, 1996 decision, 91 F.3d 1529, affirming an interlocutory injunction following partial summary judgment on ADEA liability. Monetary relief was reserved. No exact oral-argument date in this Court is established.

The questions concern independent EEOC enforcement and conciliation, employee status of working owner-directors, the age-based retirement rule and statutory exceptions, and the employment injunction's scope. Johnson & Higgins is a New Jersey corporation conducting an insurance and employee-benefits business. Its board ranges from 20 to 44 directors, with 35 at the investigation's beginning. Nomination by the chairman and election by two thirds of the board select existing senior employees; annual evaluation by six senior directors, compensation review and removal controls continue alongside substantial ownership and governance.

Directors must hold at least 500 shares, and cessation of ownership ends board service. Departure requires share sale; a ten-year agreement provides dividend-equivalent payments in exchange for consulting availability and noncompetition. Stock is predominantly director-owned, with a small fraction issued to other key employees since 1993. The unanimously adopted 1983 policy couples retirement from employment, officer status, directorship and equity at the end of the year age 62 is attained, or earlier when age 60 and fifteen board years coincide. Only the latter branch permits corporate-need extensions approved by the chairman and executive committee, year by year and no later than the end of the age-62 year.

The EEOC learned of the policy during another investigation. No current or former director sought this enforcement action, and affidavits opposed it. Investigation notice, a determination, a July 1992 conciliation meeting and invitation, renewed information requests and refusals preceded suit filed August 5, 1993. The reported releases lacked ADEA-specific and seven-day-revocation terms; no individual's monetary entitlement or release consequence is adjudicated here.

Libertarian Party of Florida v. Smith, No. 96-1867. Plenary merits decision on submission, September 21, 1998; October Term 1997, chunk 13. Review under 28 U.S.C. §1257 of the Florida Supreme Court's December 5, 1996 judgment, 687 So. 2d 1292, with rehearing denied February 17, 1997, approving the First District's judgment sustaining the filing-fee allocation. No exact oral-argument date in this Court is established.

The question is whether Florida Statutes §99.103(1) (1993) violates federal political-association and equality protections by distributing approximately half of qualifying parties' candidates' filing fees to those parties' executive committees for party expenses, while excluding parties below five percent of the State's registered voters. The criterion is objective and potentially changing; it does not name the Democratic and Republican Parties. The published description supports that approximate allocation, not an exact dollar formula.

The Libertarian Party, its executive committee and House candidate Wilson sought declaratory and injunctive relief. Wilson had qualified for the ballot; the parties concede the underlying candidate fees were lawfully collected. The challenged provision does not deny ballot access or restrict private political spending. No finding establishes that minor-party fees were specially exacted for, or directly transferred to, rival parties. The Florida Supreme Court treated the relevant state constitutional protection as coextensive with the federal protection in this case.
